faq.title: Got Questions?
faq.description: Find answers to common questions about our services, treatments, and what to expect during your recovery journey.

faqs.question: Do I need a referral to book an appointment?
faqs.answer: No referral is necessary. You can book directly through our website or by calling our clinic. We welcome selfreferrals and work with most health insurance providers.

faqs.question: What should I bring to my first visit?
faqs.answer: Please bring your ID, insurance card, any relevant medical records or imaging results, and a list of current medications. Comfortable clothing is recommended.

faqs.question: How do I schedule an appointment?
faqs.answer: You can book online through our website or call us directly. Sameday appointments are often available for urgent cases.

faqs.question: How long does each session typically last?
faqs.answer: Initial assessments are 60 minutes. Followup treatment sessions are usually 4560 minutes depending on your condition and treatment plan.

faqs.question: Is physiotherapy treatment painful?
faqs.answer: Physiotherapy should not be significantly painful. You may experience mild discomfort during treatment as we work on tight or injured tissues, but we always work within your comfort level.

faqs.question: What should I wear to my session?
faqs.answer: Wear comfortable, loosefitting clothing that allows easy access to the area being treated. For lower body issues, shorts work best. For upper body, a tank top or loose tshirt is ideal.

faqs.question: Do you accept insurance?
faqs.answer: Yes, we accept most major insurance plans. Contact our office with your insurance information and we'll verify your coverage and benefits before your appointment.

faqs.question: What are your payment options?
faqs.answer: We accept cash, major credit & debit cards and Bank Transfer. Payment plans are available for those without insurance coverage.

faqs.question: Will my insurance cover all treatments?
faqs.answer: Coverage varies by plan. Most insurance covers a certain number of physical therapy visits per year. We'll help you understand your benefits during your first visit.

faqs.question: How many sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: This varies widely depending on your condition. Some patients see significant improvement in 46 sessions, while chronic or complex conditions may require longer treatment plans.

faqs.question: Will I get exercises to do at home?
faqs.answer: Yes! Home exercises are a crucial part of your recovery. We provide personalized exercise programs and can send video demonstrations to your phone.

faqs.question: Is physiotherapy the same as chiropractic care?
faqs.answer: While there are overlaps, physiotherapy focuses on rehabilitation, movement reeducation, and exercise therapy in addition to manual techniques, offering a more comprehensive approach.

combineTreatments.question: Can I combine treatments?

postOpPackages.question: Do you offer postop packages?

neckPain.title: Neck Pain & Cervical Spondylosis
neckPain.metaDescription: Expert treatment for neck pain and cervical spondylosis. We address the root cause  sustained load and unvarying posture.
neckPain.heroSubtitle: You've adapted around it long enough.
neckPain.overview: Cervical Spondylosis is not a disease. It is an adaptation. When the neck is subjected to constant, unvarying loadsoften from sustained screen time or poor ergonomicsthe structures adapt. Discs narrow. Facet joints undergo changes. Muscles designed for movement are forced into roles of sustained stabilization, leading to fatigue, guarding, and pain.
symptoms: A deep, persistent ache that intensifies as the day progresses
Restricted rotation  difficulty checking blind spots while driving
Headaches originating at the base of the skull
Tightness or tingling radiating into the shoulders, jaw, or arms

discProlapse.heroSubtitle: The pain is in your leg. The problem is in your spine.
discProlapse.overview: The intervertebral disc is designed to withstand massive force. But when movement mechanics are flawedwhen the hips lack mobility or the deep core lacks controlthe spine absorbs repetitive, uncontrolled shear and compression. Eventually, the outer wall of the disc compromises, encroaching on sensitive neural structures nearby, creating the burning, traveling pain known as sciatica.

Can't find a position  sitting hurts, standing hurts, lying down barely helps
Foot feels numb or heavy, like it belongs to someone else

dryNeedling.title: Dry Needling
dryNeedling.metaDescription: Precision dry needling to reset the nervous system and release chronic muscle guarding from the inside out.
dryNeedling.heroSubtitle: Resetting the nervous system from the inside out.
dryNeedling.overview: When tissues are injured or overloaded, muscles enter a state of chronic guarding, developing trigger points. The nervous system becomes hypersensitized. Dry needling inserts fine solid filament needles directly into overactive muscles, creating a localized microlesion that triggers increased blood flow and forces a neurophysiological 'reset.'

Tendon sensitivity during movement

Need for support without restricting movement

neurodynamics.title: Neurodynamics
neurodynamics.metaDescription: Restoring nerve mobility through precise, graded mobilizations. When nerves get trapped, traditional stretching makes it worse.
neurodynamics.heroSubtitle: Nerves are designed to slide and glide.
neurodynamics.overview: Conditions like sciatica or cervical radiculopathy are issues of nerve mobility. Due to injury, inflammation, sustained posture, or postsurgical scar tissue, a nerve can lose its mechanical mobility. When a trapped nerve is stretched, it sends alarm signals and forces surrounding muscles into severe protective guarding.
symptoms: Tingling, numbness, or burning sensations traveling down an arm or leg
Heavy, deadfeeling limbs
Sharp, radiating pain triggered by specific movements
Severe protective muscle spasms
clinicalApproach: Neural Tension Assessment: Identifying exactly where the nerve is mechanically restricted
Graded Mobilizations: Precise, directionsensitive techniques applied to the nerve and surrounding tissue
Nerve Glides/Flossing: Restoring mechanical freedom without triggering alarm responses
Guarding Pattern Resolution: Breaking the cycle of protective muscle spasm

Nerve Glides/Flossing: Restoring mechanical freedom without triggering alarm responses

Moving your neck or limb without bracing against the electric sensation
Sleeping in positions that were previously off-limits
Understanding why the stretching you were doing was making it worse
A nervous system that allows movement instead of alarming at it
idealFor: Patients experiencing sciatica or cervical radiculopathy
Postsurgical scar tissue restricting nerve mobility
neurodynamics.whatToExpect: We use precise, graded, directionsensitive mobilizations applied directly to the nerve and its surrounding tissue to restore mechanical freedom without triggering protective alarm responses.
neurodynamics.outcome: Restored mechanical mobility of the nervous system, reduced neural sensitivity, and a permanent break in the cycle of protective muscle guarding.

injuryPrevention.title: Injury Prevention
injuryPrevention.metaDescription: Identify silent compensations before tissue failure. The most effective time to treat an injury is before it happens.
injuryPrevention.heroSubtitle: The most effective time to treat an injury is before the tissue fails.
injuryPrevention.overview: Injuries rarely happen out of nowhere. They are the climax of training volume exceeding tissue capacity, paired with poor movement mechanics. The body creates compensatory patterns to achieve tasks, but these compensations load the wrong tissues. Without adequate recovery, structural failure is inevitable.
symptoms: The same area keeps getting strained, taped, and rested  then strained again
Something feels off in your movement but your scans are clean
You're training harder than ever and getting less out of it
One side feels subtly different  not painful, just not the same
You've had one significant injury and you're quietly terrified of the next one

Force plate or singleleg load testing to identify limb dominance deficits

Written risk profile with objective rescreening timeline

returnToPlay.title: Return to Play & Performance
returnToPlay.metaDescription: Clinical recovery is not athletic readiness. Objective testing to bridge the gap between 'healed' and 'ready.'
returnToPlay.heroSubtitle: Clinical recovery is not athletic readiness.
returnToPlay.overview: The gap between 'healed' and 'ready' is where most reinjuries occur. Premature clearance is often based on pain resolution or elapsed time. Under the stress of fatigue and highspeed demands, the brain reverts to compensatory strategies if true neuromuscular control hasn't been objectively rebuilt and tested.
symptoms: Hesitation or lack of trust in the injured joint
At full speed or under fatigue, the old movement pattern comes back
One leg is measurably weaker  you feel it even if no one else sees it
Psychological fear of reinjury

Reactive agility and deceleration testing under sportspecific fatigue
Hop, jump, and cutting mechanics analysis before contact clearance

Progressive sportspecific loading with objective go/nogo criteria at each stage
Coach and trainer communication on reintegration timeline and load limits

womensHealth.title: Women's Health Physiotherapy

prenatalPostnatal.title: Pre & Postnatal Physiotherapy

geriatricMobility.title: Geriatric Mobility & Fall Prevention
geriatricMobility.metaDescription: Aging is inevitable. Decline is not. We restore reaction time, rebuild strength, and eradicate the fear of falling.
geriatricMobility.heroSubtitle: Aging is inevitable. Decline is not.
geriatricMobility.overview: Agerelated decline in mobility is rarely just about joints getting older. It is a compounding cycle of underloading. Muscle mass decreases, reaction times slow, and the nervous system loses its sharp edge. When a joint lacks muscular support, it hurts. When it hurts, we move less. When we move less, we lose the capacity to balance and catch ourselves.
symptoms: Unsteadiness on stairs, curbs, or uneven ground
Severe morning stiffness and rapid fatigue
A profound, quiet fear of falling that begins to dictate daily choices
Walking on unfamiliar surfaces or in the dark feels genuinely risky

Proprioception retraining for uneven, dark, and unpredictable surfaces

ergonomics.title: Ergonomics & Workplace Health

ergonomics.heroSubtitle: Your workstation should support your output, not break your body down.

When you sit at a poorly positioned screen or keyboard for 8 to 10 hours, you subject your neck, shoulders, and lower back to unvarying mechanical load. Muscles fatigue, joints compress, and chronic pain sets in, disrupting focus and productivity.

posturalEducation.title: Postural Education

posturalEducation.heroSubtitle: Posture is not just about how you sit.
posturalEducation.overview: Poor posture is an accumulation of physical adaptations to sustained daily demands. Over time, chest and anterior muscles become short and restricted, while the upper back and deep neck stabilizers become overstretched and weak. This imbalance compromises everything from breathing mechanics to athletic force production.

One shoulder visibly higher, one hip further forward  and it's getting more pronounced
Breathing that's shallow, neckdriven, and exhausting by end of day
Pain that shifts around rather than staying in one place  today the neck, tomorrow the midback

osteoporosis.title: Osteoporosis & Bone Health
osteoporosis.metaDescription: Building resilient bones through intelligent, targeted loading. Safely reducing fracture risk with deliberate programming.
osteoporosis.heroSubtitle: Building resilient bones requires intelligent, targeted loading.
osteoporosis.overview: Osteoporosis occurs when bone resorption outpaces bone formation, leading to reduced bone mineral density. This is driven by hormonal changes, poor nutrition, and crucially, insufficient skeletal loading. Bones respond to forces placed upon them (Wolff's Law). Without adequate resistance and impact, they become porous, fragile, and highly susceptible to fracture.

You're perimenopausal and no one has talked to you about what that means for your bones
Often completely silent until a devastating fracture occurs
Gradual loss of height over time
An increasing thoracic kyphosis (rounding of the upper back)

Progressive resistance training dosed to stimulate osteoblast activity
Safe impact exercise integration  jumping and landing mechanics for bone stimulus
Spinal extension strengthening to counter kyphotic progression

postFractureRehab.title: PostFracture Rehabilitation
postFractureRehab.metaDescription: True rehabilitation means restoring total body strength, mechanics, and confidence after a fracture  ensuring it never happens again.
postFractureRehab.heroSubtitle: Healing the bone is only the first step.
postFractureRehab.overview: When a bone fractures, immobilization is required to heal. But this immobilization causes profound secondary issues: massive muscle atrophy, joint stiffness, and heavily altered movement mechanics. Furthermore, if the fracture was caused by a fall or poor neuromuscular control, the underlying issue still remains.
symptoms: The cast came off weeks ago. The stiffness hasn't.
You're protecting the limb without realising it  and the rest of your body is starting to feel it
Muscle that visibly disappeared during immobilisation and hasn't come back
Compensatory pain in other areas (e.g., midback pain after a wrist fracture)

Joint range of motion restoration  targeting the contracture left by immobilisation
Progressive resistance to rebuild the muscle mass lost in cast
Proprioception and balance retraining for the affected limb
Compensatory pain assessment  identifying and correcting secondary load patterns
Fracture cause investigation: bone quality, biomechanics, or both
